Information moves at lightning speed, we swipe through social media, skim articles, watch reels, and jump between tasks faster than ever. Compared to a few decades ago when we consumed information through books, newspapers, and scheduled TV programs, our relationship with attention and focus has fundamentally changed. But is this shift making us more distracted, or even leading to ADHD-like behaviors?

The Information Overload Effect

Struggling with this has had a big impact on my productivity, especially when starting something new. I tend to multitask and take in too much information at once, which often leaves me either stuck and unable to start or struggling with reduced comprehension and efficiency.

Our brains are wired to seek novelty, but the modern digital environment pushes this to the extreme. With endless scrolling and constant notifications, our attention is constantly being pulled in multiple directions. A study published in The Guardian noted that "our ability to focus has been in decline for years, and the internet’s design only amplifies this trend" (source).

In the past, consuming information required patience reading a book, waiting for the evening news, or sitting through a lecture. Now, we are exposed to more content in a single hour than someone in the 19th century would have encountered in an entire week. This shift has led some experts to question whether the digital age is creating an "ADHD-like" state in many people

ADHD vs. Digital Distraction

ADHD (Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder) is a neurodevelopmental condition with genetic and neurological roots. It has existed long before smartphones or social media. However, studies suggest that modern technology may be amplifying behaviors commonly associated with ADHD, such as difficulty focusing, impulsivity, and constant task-switching.

Research published by Bournemouth University found a strong connection between ADHD symptoms and technology addiction in adults. According to Dr. John McAlaney, one of the study’s lead researchers, "we are seeing a cycle where technology use reinforces attention difficulties, making it harder to focus on tasks that require sustained effort" (source).

Similarly, a PubMed review of longitudinal studies found that excessive digital media use can exacerbate ADHD-like symptoms in children and adolescents, especially when exposure begins at an early age (source).

The Impact on Productivity and Learning

With so many distractions, it’s no surprise that productivity and learning are affected. Many people find it harder to read long articles or focus on deep work without reaching for their phones. A recent study published by New York Post revealed that despite having unlimited entertainment options, people are reporting higher levels of boredom and restlessness than ever before (source).

Some researchers argue that this is because the ability to process information quickly doesn't necessarily translate to better comprehension. While we may feel productive jumping between multiple sources of information, true learning and problem-solving require deep focus and uninterrupted thought.

Can We Rewire Our Attention?

It took me some time to realize that I needed to work on my attention span. I knew it wasn’t ADHD, but I was struggling to concentrate and needed to make some changes.

The good news is that attention is trainable. Just as technology has shaped our focus habits, we can reshape them by being more intentional with how we engage with information.

The first step to regaining your attention is recognizing that you’ve lost control of it.

These are the few things that have worked for me;

  • Mindful Consumption: Reducing screen time, taking intentional breaks, and practicing deep reading has helped me rebuild focus.
  • Single-Tasking Over Multitasking: Focusing on one task at a time, rather than juggling multiple distractions, improves cognitive performance.
  • Digital Detoxing: Start limiting notifications and carving out screen-free time daily. It’s like giving your brain a little reset and could help you stay focused for longer periods.
  • Building Attention Resilience: Activities like meditation, journaling, and even embracing boredom can strengthen focus and patience.

While the new(digital) age isn’t causing ADHD, it is reshaping the way we process information, making distractions feel like the new normal. As we continue to adapt to this environment, it’s crucial to be mindful of how it affects our ability to focus, learn, and engage deeply with the world around us.

Perhaps the real challenge isn’t whether technology is "giving" us ADHD, but whether we can reclaim our attention in an age designed to steal it.

I got distracted so many times while writing this, but I’m determined to get back on track. If this sounds familiar, take this as your little nudge to keep going. Stay strong!
